summary: Initial scoping with Cygnus Health on model selection and deployment constraints. Key drivers: PHI compliance (HIPAA-like), long-context summaries from patient histories (2-6k tokens), Spanish/Portuguese support, and tool-calling into EHR and lab-result APIs. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs, fallback routing, caching, and expected QPS. Agreed next steps: security docs, benchmark plan, and POC scheduling.
topics: latency vs cost and batching/kv cache strategies
transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2027-11-04
Start: 15:30 PST
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Ava Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Martins (Redwood SE), Maya Patel (Cygnus Head of ML), Ethan Ross (CTO), Dr. Lina Gomez (Clinical Lead), Samir Khan (Infra)

[00:00] Ava Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. we'll do a quick intros, and then Diego will jump into the technical questions. how's that sound?
[00:05] Maya Patel: Sounds great, thanks Ava. quick note, we're on an abbreviated agenda — we want to validate model fit vs deployment constraints.
[00:12] Ethan Ross: Hi all, CTO here. high level we need to understand PHI constraints and whether we can use hosted or need private.
[00:20] Diego Martins: cool, thanks. first quick question — what's your typical context length for patient notes? is it like single-visit, or multi-visit summaries?
[00:28] Dr. Lina Gomez: most of the time multi-visit. a single patient summary can be 1,500 to 6,000 tokens depending on included labs and prior visits, sometimes with attachments like imaging notes. we often need whole-encounter context for accurate summarization.
[00:45] Samir Khan: also note we are multi-region, with a lot of spanish-speaking clinics in the southwest and a small latin america pilot — so multilingual is a must.
[01:00] Diego Martins: got it. that pushes toward models with long-context capability. we discussed options: Llama 2 variants, Mistral long-context, and some of the newer open long-context models. any preference for hallucination resistance vs cost?
[01:17] Maya Patel: accuracy is paramount — false medical statements are a no-go. but we also care about throughput. our daily QPS for summarization is modest — maybe 20 to 80 requests per minute, but each request is heavy.
[01:30] Ava Chen: that's a helpful vector — accuracy first, then throughput. hosting choices: with hosted Redwood you get fastest time to value but PHI concerns; Dedicated provides isolated GPU pools and predictable performance; Private (VPC or on-prem) gives you full control over data residency and KMS.
[01:48] Ethan Ross: our legal team leans private due to PHI. but can you clarify what private means — is it customer-managed control plane always on-prem, or VPC peering with Redwood control plane?
[01:58] Diego Martins: two patterns — VPC mode where control plane is segregated and we respect VPC peering and bring-your-own-KMS; and on-prem where the runtime can be delivered as a package and we keep data completely air-gapped. for HIPAA-like compliance we usually see customers go VPC or on-prem for initial pilots.
[02:18] Maya Patel: ok that helps. for models, we need tool-calling to EHR and lab-result APIs — can Redwood call out to our systems or do we push the data into the model?
[02:30] Diego Martins: we support tool-calling / function calling patterns. common approach is lightweight retrieval + tool invocation: model emits a structured call (e.g., fetch-lab-results patient-id) and Redwood SE can wire that into a connector to your EHR. works with hosted/dedicated/private but for PHI we recommend private connectors in your VPC.
[02:52] Ethan Ross: latency for tool-calling matters — how do you manage round trips and batching?
[02:58] Diego Martins: latency is two parts — model generation and the external tool. we recommend prefetching via retrieval where possible to avoid synchronous round trips. Redwood also supports smart batching and KV cache; for multi-visit summaries we can cache patient prefix tokens (KV cache) so repeated requests for the same patient use warm cache and reduce tokens.
[03:20] Dr. Lina Gomez: what about tokenization and numeric precision for labs? sometimes units and dates matter.
[03:25] Diego Martins: good point — structured outputs and system prompts can enforce unit normalization; we also support tool outputs that are structured JSON so the model doesn't hallucinate numbers.
[03:38] Maya Patel: can you walk through a recommended model? like which open model would you start with for our use case?
[03:45] Diego Martins: sure. general starter shortlist: a 32k-context model for accuracy — options like Mistral Long-Context (32k), Llama 3-32k from community forks, and newer longform models. for highest safety, we recommend a sequence: run high-precision model for extraction/QA (bigger FP32 or Q4_0 quantized where quality is kept), and a smaller quantized generator for lower-cost tasks. we can provide quantitative benchmarks on hallucination and medical accuracy.
[04:12] Ethan Ross: what about hallucination mitigation? do you recommend retrieval augmented generation (RAG) or chain-of-thought style prompts?
[04:20] Ava Chen: RAG with strict retrieval from verified EHR docs is our standard approach, plus evaluation harnesses. Redwood Optimize gives recommendation on quantization and caching tuned to your workload.
[04:31] Samir Khan: earlier you mentioned throughput. if we need to process batch nightly for 100k records, what's the play — dedicated reserved GPUs or private on-prem cluster?
[04:42] Diego Martins: batch-heavy workloads with lower latency requirements often map well to Dedicated reserved capacity where you can have predictable throughput and autoscaling. On-prem can work too but requires more ops. For a hybrid, some customers put nightly batch on Dedicated and live inference in VPC.
[04:58] Maya Patel: curious — are there tradeoffs with continuous batching for long-context inputs? won't batching increase memory usage?
[05:06] Diego Martins: yes batching large contexts drives memory. our runtime uses continuous batching with dynamic kernel selection and can shard KV cache across GPUs. we can tune batch sizes and sequence packing to balance latency and throughput. often we recommend smaller micro-batches for tail-latency sensitive endpoints.
[05:26] Ethan Ross: any hard numbers you can share now for 32k context latency on an A100-like instance?
[05:32] Diego Martins: rough order of magnitude: for autoregressive generation with 32k context and a 1k-token reply, latencies can range from 300ms/token to 1s/token depending on model and quantization; we'll provide concrete numbers after benchmarking with your prompts.
[05:50] Maya Patel: that's a wide range. we'd need to see benchmarks because in production we can't have >200ms token latencies for interactive clinician tooling.
[05:59] Ava Chen: noted — SE-led POC will benchmark specific models for your constraint (interactive <200ms/token) and also show cost tradeoffs.
[06:10] Dr. Lina Gomez: for multilingual support, do you recommend monolingual fine-tuned models or a single multilingual model?
[06:16] Diego Martins: depends on volume. single multilingual models can work well, but if you have high volume in Spanish with specific clinical shorthand, fine-tuning or instruction-tuning on Spanish clinical corpus yields better accuracy. we also support per-tenant fine-tuning in Private deployments.
[06:34] Samir Khan: how do you handle encryption and key management in VPC mode?
[06:38] Diego Martins: in VPC mode we support BYOK via KMS/HSM and never send plaintext logs to our control plane. audit logs can be pushed to your log sinks. we also have options for HSM-backed signing for model weights if needed.
[06:50] Ethan Ross: does Redwood provide SOC2 docs and a security whitepaper?
[06:53] Ava Chen: yes, we'll share SOC2 and our security appendix. I'll add that to next steps.
[06:58] Maya Patel: i'd like to talk about evaluation — how do you measure medical hallucinations quantitatively?
[07:04] Diego Martins: we use targeted evals (precision/recall on extraction), clinical QA datasets, and custom prompt sets. Redwood allows tying regression alerts to prompt sets so we detect drift post-deploy.
[07:20] Ava Chen: quick check — any regulatory geo-constraints? do you need EU-only hosting?
[07:25] Maya Patel: not yet but possibly for future partners in EU we might need data residency.
[07:30] Diego Martins: that's doable — we have multi-region routing and can pin inference to region-specific capacity.
[07:36] Ethan Ross: a question on costs — if we use a 32k-context model with KV cache, how much does caching help cost per token?
[07:44] Diego Martins: caching helps a lot for repeated patient prefixes. savings vary but we've seen 30-60% token savings when the same history is reused. precise numbers depend on repetition in your workload.
[07:58] Samir Khan: for tool-calling, do you have examples of schema enforcement so the model doesn't call random endpoints?
[08:05] Diego Martins: yes, function calling with strict schemas and a gateway layer that only exposes allowed operations. plus audit logs for calls.
[08:12] Dr. Lina Gomez: that's good. what about prompt engineering support? we don't have a big prompt ops team.
[08:17] Ava Chen: our Solutions Engineering team helps with prompt tuning, eval harness setup, and example-driven instruction templates as part of the POC.
[08:25] Maya Patel: ok, let's drill into a POC scope — what would you propose?
[08:29] Diego Martins: propose 3-week POC: week 1 data wrangling + sample prompt set and security onboarding; week 2 bench & RAG integration; week 3 live testing and tuning. deliverables: benchmark report, config suggestions for batching/quant, and a runbook for deployment path (hosted/dedicated/private).
[08:50] Ethan Ross: timeline-wise we want to start pilot before end of year. is that feasible?
[08:55] Ava Chen: yes, if we get security docs and dataset snippets this week we can kick POC mid-November.
[09:03] Maya Patel: one more technical: how are model updates handled? we need stable versioning for audits.
[09:09] Diego Martins: Redwood supports model pinning, versioned rollouts, canary, and automatic fallback to previous pinned versions. audit logs include model version and token metrics.
[09:22] Samir Khan: any limitations on tool-calling frequency? like rate limits for function calls that go to EHR?
[09:29] Diego Martins: rate limits are configurable per route; for private we push rate controls to your VPC connectors to avoid throttling.
[09:36] Dr. Lina Gomez: what about human-in-the-loop? can we route uncertain cases to a clinician queue before sending to patient portal?
[09:43] Ava Chen: yes — we can add confidence thresholds and route to review queues. Redwood Console exposes per-route thresholds and alerting.
[09:52] Ethan Ross: competitors — we've evaluated OpenAI and Anthropic; how do you compare on latency, cost, and private deployment?
[09:59] Diego Martins: high level: OpenAI excels at managed quality but has constraints on private deployments. Anthropic also strong on safety. Redwood differentiator is production runtime flexibility — unified API across hosted/dedicated/private plus focused tooling for caching/batching and model lifecycle controls that reduce unit economics in production.
[10:20] Maya Patel: can you share any healthcare customer case study or redacted benchmarks?
[10:25] Ava Chen: yes we'll share a redacted benchmark and a healthcare reference architecture (anonymized).
[10:30] Samir Khan: about observability — can we get token-level cost breakouts and per-route latencies?
[10:35] Diego Martins: yes the Console provides token-level cost, latency heatmaps, and per-model breakdowns. we can add tracing hooks to logs.
[10:43] Maya Patel: regarding model fine-tuning — is there an option for private fine-tuning on-prem?
[10:47] Diego Martins: yes, private deployments support per-tenant fine-tuning workflows. in some cases we do instruction-tuning rather than full fine-tune to reduce footprint.
[10:56] Ethan Ross: for the POC, what's the billing model? trial credits or committed pricing?
[11:01] Ava Chen: typically we provide trial credits and for Dedicated we discuss reserved capacity contracts. we'll include pricing in the follow-up.
[11:08] Maya Patel: sounds good. let's recap action items.
[11:12] Ava Chen: recap: Ava will send SOC2/security docs and pricing; Diego will draft POC plan and sample prompts; Maya will send redacted sample notes and confirm timelines. schedule POC kickoff for 2027-11-16.
[11:28] Ethan Ross: thanks everyone.
[11:30] Meeting ended.
